title: Avianca 4
summary: Avianca Flight 03 crashed shortly after takeoff from Cartagena on January 14, 1966. The aircraft reached 100 ft, then stalled and crashed into shallow water near the runway. After a 14-month investigation, engine failure was suspected but remained unproven, with poor maintenance and inadequate inspections also noted.

title: Air India 101
summary: Air India Flight 101, a Boeing 707 named Kanchenjunga, crashed into Mont Blanc in France on 24 January 1966 while on approach to Geneva. The pilot, thinking he had passed Mont Blanc, started to descend and flew into the Mont Blanc massif at 4750 meters elevation. All 117 people aboard were killed.
probable_cause: The pilot believed the aircraft had passed Mont Blanc when instructed to descend for Geneva, but the aircraft had not yet cleared the mountain. The crew had one VOR receiver unserviceable and failed to confirm their position before descending.

title: Lufthansa 005
summary: Lufthansa Flight 005 was on final approach to Bremen in fog, heavy rain, and darkness with a 6-knot tailwind exceeding the 5-knot maximum. An instrument displayed false information causing the aircraft to deviate from the ILS glide path. The captain estimated altitude incorrectly during the transition from instruments to visual control. At approximately 10 meters above ground, the captain commenced a go-around but maneuvered the aircraft into an extreme flight attitude causing a stall. The aircraft spun left, struck the ground with its left wing, and crashed 400 meters beyond the runway end.
probable_cause: The crash was caused by a chain of technical and human errors. An instrument displayed false information causing deviation from the ILS glide path. The captain's altitude estimate was incorrect due to darkness and poor visibility. The captain maneuvered the aircraft into an extreme flight attitude during the go-around, causing a stall from which recovery was impossible.

events.text: The flight began its approach from the east to runway 27 at the Bremen Airport in ceiling less than 100 m and visibility approximately 700 m.
The aircraft descended through clouds in heavy rain and darkness with a 6-knot tailwind exceeding the maximum of 5 knots.

Captain Heinz Saalfeld commenced a go-around maneuver at an approximate height of 10 m above the ground.
A few moments later the aircraft spun to the left and crashed into a field 400 m beyond the end of the runway.

title: All Nippon Airways 60
summary: All Nippon Airways Flight 60, a Boeing 727-81, departed Sapporo bound for Tokyo on 4 February 1966 with 126 passengers and a crew of seven. While on night approach to Haneda Airport in clear weather approximately 10.4 kilometers from the airport, the aircraft crashed into Tokyo Bay. The pilot had announced intention to land visually without instruments, and the aircraft subsequently disappeared from radar. The fuselage was later recovered with all bodies inside. No flight recorders were installed, and the cause of the accident was never determined.

title: Canadian Pacific Air Lines 402
summary: Flight 402, a DC-8-43 flying Hong Kong-Tokyo-Vancouver, held near Haneda for 38 minutes and cancelled one approach as visibility fluctuated below minima at night. After diverting toward Taipei and being told visibility had improved to a 3,000 ft runway visual range, the captain flew a second approach; advised the aircraft was 20 ft low near the runway, it continued below and parallel to the glide slope before a sharp descent struck eleven approach lights and the seawall short of the threshold. The pilot lost control after impact and 64 of 72 aboard were killed. Investigators found no tower fault, attributing the crash to pilot error and possible optical illusion from poor visibility.
probable_cause: "Pilot misjudged landing approach under unusually difficult weather conditions," with poor visibility cited as a possible source of an optical illusion; the investigation found no fault with the airport control tower.

factors.evidence: struck the approach lights and a seawall during a night landing attempt in poor visibility at Haneda Airport

events.text: At 19:58, after holding 38 minutes and cancelling one approach when visibility dropped, the pilot asked ATC to divert to Songshan Airport, Taiwan.
At 20:05, climbing through 11,500 ft toward Taipei, the pilot was told visibility at Haneda had improved to a runway visual range of 3,000 ft, and decided on another approach.

Advised it was 20 ft low near the runway, the aircraft nevertheless continued 20 ft below and parallel to the glide slope, and after passing the precision minimum the crew requested reduced runway light intensity.
The aircraft made a sharp descent and, 2,800 ft from the runway threshold, its landing gear struck eleven approach lights before hitting the seawall, and the pilot lost control.

title: BOAC 911
summary: BOAC Flight 911, a Boeing 707 departing Tokyo Haneda for Hong Kong, encountered severe clear-air turbulence over Mount Fuji and disintegrated in mid-air on 5 March 1966. The structural failure began with the vertical stabilizer attachment failing under extreme aerodynamic loads. All 124 occupants were killed.
probable_cause: The aircraft encountered abnormally severe clear-air turbulence over Gotemba City which imposed gust loads considerably in excess of the aircraft's structural design, causing the vertical stabilizer to fail and leading to airframe breakup in flight.

factors.evidence: the vertical stabiliser attachment to the fuselage failed first
The aircraft then encountered strong turbulence, causing it to break up in flight
The aircraft then entered a flat spin, with the forward fuselage section and the outer starboard wing breaking off shortly before impact
stress cracking was found in the vertical stabiliser bolt holes
Subsequent inspections on Boeing 707 and similar Boeing 720 aircraft revealed this was a common problem

events.text: The aircraft began taxiing at 13:50 and took off into the northwest wind at 13:58.
After takeoff, the aircraft made a continuous climbing right turn over Tokyo Bay and rolled out on a southwest heading.
At an altitude of approximately 16000 ft, well above the 12388 ft mountain peak, the aircraft encountered strong turbulence.
The vertical stabiliser attachment to the fuselage failed first, and the ventral fin and all four engine pylons failed due to leftward over-stress.
The aircraft entered a flat spin, with the forward fuselage section and the outer starboard wing breaking off shortly before impact.
Flight 911 left a debris field 16 km long after impact with the ground.

title: LANSA 501
summary: Flight 501 departed Lima at 07:40 AM and climbed on a heading of 190° until reaching 9 nm southwest of the airport, then turned toward Cusco. The crew violated the planned route by flying a direct straight route toward the mountain range. Eyewitnesses reported the aircraft flying low over San Pedro de Pilas at 8:00 AM at a heading of 100° and turning left to avoid mountains. The aircraft struck Mount Talaula around 08:05 AM at approximately the planned deviation point.
probable_cause: The crew violated the planned route regulations and flew a straight course toward Cusco, becoming unable to clear the summits due to insufficient climb performance. The captain may have overestimated the aircraft's technical abilities, with his judgment impaired by lack of rest and pre-flight preparation.

factors.evidence: The crew violated the planned route regulations provided by the airline and decided to fly a straight route from Las Palmas to Cusco instead of the prescribed routing.

The climb performance was incorrectly calculated in relation to its total weight at takeoff, meaning it may not have been able to climb to the required height to clear the high mountains within 25 minutes of flight time.
The captain had completed the previous day's duties late, it was assumed he had a rest period of only 6½ hours before the flight.
Flight 501 struck Mount Talaula around 8:05 AM PET, with the wreckage being recovered the next day and all 49 occupants killed.

events.text: Flight 501 departed Lima at 7:40 AM PET, 10 minutes later than schedule, from runway 15 instructed to climb at a heading of 190° until 9 nautical miles southwest of the airport.
At 7:57 AM PET, crew reported their position to Lima airport and stated 'Departed Lima-Callao at 1240Z, climbing, estimating Ayacucho at 1337Z.'

Shortly after 8:00 AM, eyewitnesses reported a low-flying plane over the village of San Pedro de Pilas with the 'LANSA' inscription visible, flying towards the mountain range below the peaks at a heading of 100° and turning left to avoid mountains.
Flight 501 struck Mount Talaula around 8:05 AM PET, with the wreckage found 5 nm northeast of the village, and all 49 occupants killed in the crash.

title: Braniff 250
summary: Braniff Flight 250, a BAC 1-11-203AE operating from Kansas City to Omaha, entered an area of severe thunderstorm activity with extreme turbulence. The aircraft violently accelerated upward in an updraft with a left roll, causing the right tailplane and vertical stabilizer to fail. Within one or two seconds the right wing also failed. The aircraft tumbled from the sky in flames and impacted a soybean field near Falls City, Nebraska, killing all 42 aboard. The NTSB determined the probable cause as in-flight structural failure caused by extreme turbulence during operation in an avoidable weather hazard, compounded by inaccurate company weather forecast.
probable_cause: In-flight structural failure due to extreme turbulence during operation of the aircraft in an area of avoidable hazardous weather.

title: Britannia Airways 105
summary: Bristol Britannia on final approach to Ljubljana with 117 aboard struck trees in forest southeast of Runway 31. Investigation concluded pilot-in-command failed to set altimeter to QFE pressure (968 mb) as instructed by ATC, instead using QNH (1011 mb), resulting in aircraft flying approximately 1,100 feet lower than safe procedure altitudes. Crew did not cross-check altimeters per operations manual, and visual illusion from moonlit night and forest terrain prevented recognition of critically low altitude until impact.
probable_cause: Altimeter setting error: pilot-in-command set altimeter to QNH instead of required QFE pressure value; failure to cross-check altimeter readings between pilots; crew disregarded checklist procedures and operations manual for approach and landing.

title: Ansett-ANA 149
summary: Ansett-ANA Flight 149, a Vickers Viscount, developed a fire in engine number 2 during cruise at altitude. The crew were unable to feather the propeller and made an emergency descent toward Winton. The fire spread into the wheel bay and breached the fuel tank wall in the left wing, causing structural weakness. The upper spar was critically weakened between engines 1 and 2. The aircraft crashed 13.5 nautical miles short of Winton with the left wing separating during impact.
probable_cause: The probable cause was uncontained engine failure with fire in the cabin pressurisation blower rotor, which spread to structural elements and led to loss of wing strength and structural failure.

title: West Coast Airlines 956
summary: During descent via radar vector from Seattle Center, Flight 956 received instruction to descend from 14,000 feet to 9,000 feet and turn right to heading 300 degrees. The aircraft descended to approximately 4,000 feet and leveled off in a normal descent pattern. An abrupt climb was initiated two seconds before impact. The crew had only 17 to 50 hours on the DC-9 type. The specific cause of descent below clearance limits was never determined by the NTSB.
probable_cause: The descent of the aircraft below its clearance limit and below that of surrounding obstructing terrain, but the Board was unable to determine the cause of such descent.

title: 1966 Flying Tiger Line Canadair CL-44 crash
summary: A Flying Tiger Line Canadair CL-44 carrying munitions for the US Air Force approached Da Nang Airport on December 24, 1966 in rain and foggy conditions with critically low fuel reserves. The crew continued the approach below the glide path and the aircraft struck trees at a kilometer south of the runway, crashing into Binh Thai village. All four crew members and 107 people on the ground were killed.
probable_cause: The crew continued the approach under the glide path, probably due to the poor weather conditions during the flight. The low fuel state made aborting the landing impossible.
